title: A yellow leaf (235–238)
hookLine: you are now like a withered leaf; make yourself an island, work hard, be wise
last: THE MIND IS WHERE ANGER FIRST KNOCKS.

cards: Pick up a leaf in late autumn, one of the yellow ones that let go of the branch without any wind at all. It's light, dry and a little curled, and it still has every vein in place, like a map of a life.
It was green in May. It didn't notice the change until it was nearly done. Most of us are the same: the years feel slow until one day they don't.
Chapter eighteen of the Dhammapada opens by holding up a leaf like that and saying, gently but directly, this is you. Then it tells you what to build.

teach.h: A SEAR LEAF AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: Verse two thirty-five, in Max Müller's translation: "Thou art now like a sear leaf, the messengers of death (Yama) have come near to thee; thou standest at the door of thy departure, and thou hast no provision for thy journey."
Sear is an old word for dry and withered.

The messengers of death, in the Pali, are Yama's men, death's own servants, already standing near. The picture is someone at the door, about to leave on a long trip, with no packed bag and no food for the road.
The old commentary says these verses were spoken to an old man near the end of his life, as a gentle push to make good use of what remained.
Then the answer, verse two thirty-six: "Make thyself an island, work hard, be wise!" In a flood, an island is the one piece of ground the water can't cover.
The Pali word is dīpa, the word you met on day seventy-nine, when the Buddha, near the end, told Ānanda to be islands to themselves.
Island or lamp, it can be read either way.
What this verse adds is the building material: effort and wisdom, gathered while there's still time.
None of this is meant to frighten anyone. The leaf is simply honest, and a leaf that knows it's a leaf can still do a great deal of good before it lets go.

how: Buddhists often reflect on death as a spur to practice, and the Buddha's advice to be an island to oneself is often quoted as a call to rely on one's own effort and the teaching.

o: a leaf that lets go of its branch in autumn
the supplies you pack for a long journey
solid ground in a flood: an island, or a lamp

games.q: match each image to its meaning.

s: dīpa in Pali can mean both island and lamp
translators still weigh which to use; both fit the image.
these verses are meant to frighten people about death
the commentary sets them as a gentle push to use the time that's left.
Müller's 'sear leaf' means a dry, withered leaf
sear is an old word for dry and withered.

games.q: you're standing at the door of a long journey, and you realize you have nothing packed. what does verse 236 say to do?
o: make yourself an island: work hard, be wise.
sit down and wait for someone to pack for you.
games.why: "make thyself an island, work hard, be wise!" solid ground in the flood, built while there's time.

practice: If you have a leaf nearby, hold it; if not, picture one, yellow and light in your palm, and feel, without drama, that your time is not endless.
Ask yourself what one thing that really matters you keep putting off, a conversation, a practice, a kindness, a letter, and let it come up on its own.
Hold it next to the leaf, then let both rest, and sit on your island: this breath, this ground, steady in the flood.

wordCard.voice: Dīpa. Island, and also lamp: verse two thirty-six says make yourself an island, after verse two thirty-five calls you a withered leaf at the door of departure.

orig.note: Pali: island, and also lamp — so karohi dīpam attano, make an island for yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: make an island. Effort and wisdom, while there's still time. See you tomorrow.
